main_message: America builds few ships because few orders come, not because it forgot how. Wartime government demand and Korea's export orders built big yards. The Jones Act's small protected market with high prices keeps US yards subscale, and wages are only one factor.
why_hook: The 3-ships-a-day vs 0.04% contrast is striking, and the 'wages is the lazy answer' promise plus the November 9 deadline give a reason to stay. The 0.04% figure and the 'Philadelphia is Korean' line come fast and are not explained.
people_you_remember: Henry Kaiser (wanted to grow Richmond on British orders), Chung Ju-yung (built Ulsan from nothing on a Livanos order), Josie Lucille Owens (a welder, shown only as a photo, with no motive). Senator Wesley Jones barely registers.
mechanisms_in_your_words: 1) Government or foreign orders create yards (Kaiser, Hyundai). 2) Jones Act protection limits the market to a small captive fleet. 3) The subsidy ended in the 1980s and output fell. 4) High prices cut domestic demand, there are no exports, so no scale, which keeps prices high (loop). 5) China's state-backed export machine. 6) Fees were suspended, and Hanwha is investing in Philadelphia on a Pentagon order. These stack unevenly. The subsidy and the loop are not clearly reconciled, and China is bolted on late.
ending_comment: Mostly yes: few orders, no exports, no scale. But it ends by admitting nobody measured how much each factor counts, so the 'wages' question is only half-answered. The Kaiser callback is a nice close.

boring_or_slow.why: Stat dump of days, ship counts and population in one run. The 4.5-day Peary stunt is fun, but the numbers pile up.
Long on Korean sourcing caveats (turtle ship banknote lore, Hyundai's own account) and the per-capita GDP detour. It loses momentum before the point lands.
Dates and notices pile up (March 12, April 17, October 14, November 9, a letter from 200 groups). It reads like a docket.

confusing.why: Is that 0.04% or 4%? Say '0.04 percent'. It also isn't clear it's tonnage of commercial ships, and it ignores Navy construction.

confusing.quote: federal subsidy meant to let American owners buy American ships
confusing.why: It never names the program. I assume it's Construction Differential Subsidy, and the 'world price' idea isn't explained. It also never says the CDS ended in 1981.

confusing.quote: fifteen to twenty-five new ships a year
confusing.why: Ships versus tonnage and share are mixed. Five percent of tonnage and 15-25 ships a year don't map onto each other, and the 'around five a year' figure is unclear on what is counted (large oceangoing commercial?).
It puts 3/day against 5/year as a scoreboard and then waves it off. Liberty ships were simple cargo ships. Today's output includes Navy, tugs, barges and offshore vessels.

confusing.quote: ships owned or operated by Chinese companies, and ships built in China
confusing.why: Too compressed to follow the USTR fee structure (net-tonnage or per-container, and the exemptions). A viewer can't picture what the fee was.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: the lack of exports, and the scale that comes with them
felt_biased_or_one_sided.direction: Toward the scale/orders thesis, and away from the wage and cost explanation
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: The script says the record only 'lists' wages and then leans on the loop, which it admits is its own interpretation. The cost gap rising from 20% to 300% over decades is also pretty consistent with structural productivity and labor costs, which the script plays down.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: no documents for it, so treat it as lore
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: It leans on Hyundai's self-account for the Livanos order and the 'no experience' claim, and treats those as sourced while hedging the turtle-ship story. It also skips the large role of state credit, the Korean government's guarantees and the UK financing (Barclays, Lithgow/Scott Lithgow tech transfer).

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: ninety percent of the ships Chinese shipbuilders made were for export
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: The framing is thin on the counter-argument that fees raise costs (only the Chinese ministry is quoted) and on whether fees help US shipbuilding.

lean_detail: Fairly even-handed on the Jones Act (AMP vs Lee/McClintock) and attributes everything. Slightly skeptical of the 'it's just wages' view, and sympathetic to demand-side explanations.

claims_you_doubt.why: Roughly right for Liberty/Victory/C-types in 1943, but Liberty launches alone averaged ~2 per day. Check the 'three' and whether it's counting all merchant types.

claims_you_doubt.quote: Henry J. Kaiser started his first Richmond shipyard
claims_you_doubt.why: Richmond Yard No. 1 was built for the British contract in Dec 1940, so OK. But the 'orders, not Kaiser's methods' framing undersells prefab, welding and standardization (Emergency Shipbuilding Program) that made the speed possible.

claims_you_doubt.quote: A Liberty ship took a hundred and twenty-two days... thirty-nine
claims_you_doubt.why: Plausible for the average from keel-laying to delivery, but check the definition. 'Four days and fifteen and a half hours' was keel to launch, not delivery. It's presented as a ship 'built'.
The usual number is 2,710 (2,711 in some sources). 'Over' is odd. Also 'almost eighty yards held contracts' conflates Liberty yards (18) with all Maritime Commission contractors.

claims_you_doubt.quote: requiring Alaska-bound cargo to move through the Port of Seattle
claims_you_doubt.why: Section 27 was a general cabotage rule, and the Alaska/Canada rail issue was one motivator. It also existed in the Merchant Marine Act of 1920 and earlier cabotage laws (1789, 1817 coastwise). Skipping that makes it look new, and 'American-built' dates to 1817 and 1920.

claims_you_doubt.quote: some observers see that as the main reason
claims_you_doubt.why: The CDS ended in 1981, but US shipbuilding also collapsed because of Navy cutbacks, Reagan-era Navy buildup tapering, and the rise of Asian yards. It's single-causal.

claims_you_doubt.quote: ninety-nine oceangoing ships in the Jones Act fleet
claims_you_doubt.why: That's a small, specific count (large oceangoing) and is mixed with ship-type cost multiples. 99 ships is the fleet, not the market. Tugs, barges, ferries and Great Lakes vessels are a far bigger Jones Act market.

claims_you_doubt.quote: a truck, a train or a pipeline
claims_you_doubt.why: True for some routes, but it ignores that Jones Act prices are a big deal for Hawaii, Puerto Rico and Alaska where there's no substitute.

claims_you_doubt.quote: ships built in China, owed a fee
claims_you_doubt.why: USTR's fees covered Chinese-operated and owned vessels, and a separate fee on foreign-built car carriers and any ship built in China. Check the 'based mostly on size' claim. They were on net tonnage or containers, and some small vessels were exempt.

claims_you_doubt.quote: one and a half ships a year to twenty
claims_you_doubt.why: The Philly Shipyard's actual recent output is around 1-2 ships/year (container-ship builds), so OK. But 20/year from one yard would be a huge jump, and it's presented without context on what class of ship (the 'National Security Multi-Mission Vessel' class vs bigger hulls).

questions_left_unanswered: How much do wages explain? The script promises a 'narrower' record and never gives a number or a comparison.
What about Navy shipbuilding (Huntington Ingalls, GD, ~$30B+ a year)? It's invisible and distorts the '0.04%' story.
What happened to Japan and Korea's modern productivity advantages (automation, block construction)?
Why did Korea succeed with state aid while the US subsidy (CDS) didn't generate exports?
How big is the Jones Act market for tugs, barges and offshore vessels?
Does repealing the Jones Act make yards disappear? Nothing on that counterfactual.
Why did other Western yards (Europe) also shrink?
What do the 'fee pause' and November 9 deadline concretely mean for shipbuilding here? The hook promised a deadline that the script never connects strongly.
best_moment: 03: it sets out the 'wages' explanation, then shows the cost gap going from 20% to 300% and the loop of 'high prices, few orders, no scale'. It also flags 'the loop is our interpretation', which is the most honest thing in the video.
top3_fixes: Fix the units and scope up front. Say '0.04 percent of world commercial tonnage' and add a line that US Navy shipbuilding is a separate, still-large business. Separate Liberty ship counts, tonnage and all-ship counts.

Give the 'wages' case a fair hearing with a real number, such as labor share of cost or hours-per-ton against Korea or Japan. Drop the pretense that the record rules it out. The video says the gap went from 20% to 300% and never asks what changed.

Cut dates and sourcing caveats in segs 04 and 05 by half, and spend the time on people (Josie Owens, Chung, the Hanwha deal, a Philly yard worker) and a clean plain-language explainer of the fee and the CDS subsidy.
